newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Boeing, McDonnell busy, not wild.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Boeing, McDonnell busy, not wild.

text.p: Options activity in both Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp picked up from normal levels but was not extraordinary after the companies announced plans to merge, traders said Monday.
News of the merger appeared to catch options participants by surprise, with most of the individual issues having small open interest and little recent trading.
A trader at the Pacific Stock Exchange said of trading in McDonnell Douglas options, "We had a lot of buyers on the opening and some back-and-forth paper after (the stock) settled in."
The McDonnell activity was "nothing out of the ordinary that you wouldn't see normally in a situation like this," she said.
On Sunday, Boeing and McDonnell Douglas announced a $13.3 billion stock-for-stock merger.
The news drove both share prices higher, with Boeing gaining 5-5/8 to 102-3/8 and McDonnell Douglas surging 11-1/2 to 63-1/2 by 1015 CST/1615 GMT.
Both companies were off their early session peaks.
Among the options, investors focused on the calls, most of which surged along with the stock prices. Volatilities rose in conjunction with the options, traders said.

For Boeing, the most active option was the January 100 call, which traded about 1,380 contracts by 1030 CST/1630 GMT. The option was up 2-5/8 at five and had open interest of 3,274, which included an addition of 35 last Friday.
The January 95 call traded more than 1,250 contracts and gained 4-1/4 to 8-3/4. Its open interest was 2,867.
The only other Boeing option that traded more than 1,000 contracts was the May 100 put, with volume of 1,005. Its open interest was 76.
Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co, said the May 100 trading was most likely from an arbitrageur.
The Boeing January 100 call traded 68 contracts last Friday, 222 last Thursday and 78 last Wednesday.
"There was not big volume in the out-of-the-money options, and that's where option activity would have occurred" if word of the deal had leaked out, Schwartz said.
For McDonnell Douglas options, the heaviest action was in the December 55 calls, which traded nearly 700 contracts. The option soared eight points to 8-1/4. Its open interest was 854 contracts.
The February 55 call traded about 535 contracts and rose 8-1/16 to 9-3/4.
The only significant put volume in McDonnell Douglas was in the January 60s, which traded nearly 200 contracts.
"The options market is taking a ho-hum attitude" toward the deal, Schwartz said.
The Boeing call activity suggested that investors were not expecting much stock price appreciation, he said.
Also, the length of time required for government approval of the deal inhibits short-term trading opportunities in options, he said.
Boeing said it expected the deal to close in six months. ((G.Crawford, 312 408 8750/Email: derivatives@reuters.com))
